[Ronice Quadros](https://independent.academia.edu/RoniceQuadros)

Frontiers in Psychology, 2014

Bilingual children develop sensitivity to the language used by their interlocutors at an early age, reflected in differential use of each language by the child depending on their interlocutor. Factors such as discourse context and relative language dominance in the community may mediate the degree of language differentiation in preschool age children. Bimodal bilingual children, acquiring both a sign language and a spoken language, have an even more complex situation. Their Deaf parents vary considerably in access to the spoken language. Furthermore, in addition to code-mixing and code-switching, they use code-blending-expressions in both speech and sign simultaneously-an option uniquely available to bimodal bilinguals. Code-blending is analogous to code-switching sociolinguistically, but is also a way to communicate without suppressing one language. For adult bimodal bilinguals, complete suppression of the non-selected language is cognitively demanding. We expect that bimodal bilingual children also find suppression difficult, and use blending rather than suppression in some contexts. We also expect relative community language dominance to be a factor in children's language choices. This study analyzes longitudinal spontaneous production data from four bimodal bilingual children and their Deaf and hearing interlocutors. Even at the earliest observations, the children produced more signed utterances with Deaf interlocutors and more speech with hearing interlocutors. However, while three of the four children produced >75% speech alone in speech target sessions, they produced <25% sign alone in sign target sessions. All four produced bimodal utterances in both, but more frequently in the sign sessions, potentially because they find suppression of the dominant language more difficult. Our results indicate that these children are sensitive to the language used by their interlocutors, while showing considerable influence from the dominant community language.

What explains the differences in phonological processing between bilinguals and monolinguals?add

The study finds that exposure to two languages enhances bilinguals' phonological discrimination abilities, allowing for better adaptability in phonemic tasks compared to monolingual peers (TDB vs LIB, age 8:6). This aligns with dynamic systems theory, highlighting the interaction between language exposure and phonological development.

How do typically developing bilinguals perform on nonword repetition tasks compared to peers with language impairment?add

Results indicate that typically developing bilinguals consistently outperform their peers with language impairment on nonword repetition tasks, with a significant gap observed throughout the study ages (TDB vs LIB scores, age 4;8). This task appears reliable in diagnosing bilingual language impairment.

What role does socio-economic status play in bilingual vocabulary development?add

The research demonstrates that socio-economic status significantly influences the richness and complexity of language input, affecting bilingual children's vocabulary growth (TDB and LIB's vocabulary scores across socio-economic backgrounds). This highlights that language development must be viewed through the lens of environmental context.

When do bilingual children typically differentiate their languages in social interactions?add

Evidence suggests bilingual children begin to distinguish their languages and apply appropriate sociolinguistic conventions by age three, impacting their communication and Theory of Mind abilities (LIB's assessment outcomes, age 8:6). This illustrates early cognitive and linguistic skill interdependence.

How is communicative ability assessed in bilingual children with and without language impairment?add

The study's prototype screening tool utilizes a holistic model of communicative ability, evaluating linguistic, discourse, interactional, sociocultural, strategic, and monitoring skills (score distributions of TDB vs LIB). It emphasizes the need for varied assessments to prevent misdiagnosis.

## Abstract

![Image 10: sparkles](https://c.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)
AI

This study explores the dynamic communicative abilities in typically developing bilingual (TDB) children compared to children with bilingual language impairment (LIB) through a longitudinal twin case study. Findings indicate that TDB and LIB exhibit different patterns of language acquisition, particularly regarding noun inflections and verb aspects in Polish, suggesting that linguistic development is influenced by bilingual status and exposure. The research highlights the need for independent assessment norms for bilingual children and underscores the interaction between communicative ability and environmental influences.

Bilingualism is can be considered, in many cases, a reality in our modern society. Each day more and more bilingual families, schools and communities arise, and this scenario proposes a new approach to families, educators and society as a whole, and requires from the scientific society the development of more studies on the field. In that sense, this work aims to analyze language acquisition in early childhood bilingual education. The general objective we aim to analyze is whether the nonseparation of codes in a child’s speech environment would negatively affect his or her productive skills in either one or both languages; a problem already discussed by other researchers, such as Huerta-Macías (1983). Our specific objectives are: (1) To follow the linguistic development of bilingual children in the age of language acquisition (1-3 years old), (2) to observe if the children differentiate, sociolinguistically, between the two languages, (3) to understand how the two languages interact linguistically in their speech and (4) to analyze if the Portuguese language is going to interfere better in the English language production. For that, we will be based on the studies in the field of bilingualism from Ueno (2011), Butler and Hakuta (2004), Ramos (2004), Bialystok (2001), De Houwe (2005), Bialystok and Hakuta (1994), Escobedo (1983), Huerta-Macías (1983); and language development from Vygostky (1962,1978). Understanding that it is unfeasible to analyze a big amount of bilingual children, the corpus of this research will be twins that have been brought up bilingually since the age of 3 months by their mother, who is a teacher of English. However, she did not follow strictly the one language-one person” principle, for the mother would vary from speaking English and Portuguese with the children in different contexts and situations. We will focus on their language acquisition process from the ages 1 to 3 years old. Data was collected through video recording. We conclude that the children analyzed can be considered early, and unbalanced bilingual, according to the classification of Butler and Hakuta (2004) and that the development of a speech pattern came from their own growing sociolinguistic awareness.

Bilingual children develop sensitivity to the language used by their interlocutors at an early age, reflected in differential use of each language by the child depending on their interlocutor. Factors such as discourse context and relative language dominance in the community may mediate the degree of language differentiation in preschool age children. Bimodal bilingual children, acquiring both a sign language and a spoken language, have an even more complex situation. Their Deaf parents vary considerably in access to the spoken language. Furthermore, in addition to code-mixing and code-switching, they use code-blending-expressions in both speech and sign simultaneously-an option uniquely available to bimodal bilinguals. Code-blending is analogous to code-switching sociolinguistically, but is also a way to communicate without suppressing one language. For adult bimodal bilinguals, complete suppression of the non-selected language is cognitively demanding. We expect that bimodal bilingual children also find suppression difficult, and use blending rather than suppression in some contexts. We also expect relative community language dominance to be a factor in children's language choices. This study analyzes longitudinal spontaneous production data from four bimodal bilingual children and their Deaf and hearing interlocutors. Even at the earliest observations, the children produced more signed utterances with Deaf interlocutors and more speech with hearing interlocutors. However, while three of the four children produced >75% speech alone in speech target sessions, they produced <25% sign alone in sign target sessions. All four produced bimodal utterances in both, but more frequently in the sign sessions, potentially because they find suppression of the dominant language more difficult. Our results indicate that these children are sensitive to the language used by their interlocutors, while showing considerable influence from the dominant community language.

Results indicate that typically developing bilinguals consistently outperform their peers with language impairment on nonword repetition tasks, with a significant gap observed throughout the study ages (TDB vs LIB scores, age 4;8). This task appears reliable in diagnosing bilingual language impairment.

What role does socio-economic status play in bilingual vocabulary development?add

The research demonstrates that socio-economic status significantly influences the richness and complexity of language input, affecting bilingual children's vocabulary growth (TDB and LIB's vocabulary scores across socio-economic backgrounds). This highlights that language development must be viewed through the lens of environmental context.

When do bilingual children typically differentiate their languages in social interactions?add

Evidence suggests bilingual children begin to distinguish their languages and apply appropriate sociolinguistic conventions by age three, impacting their communication and Theory of Mind abilities (LIB's assessment outcomes, age 8:6). This illustrates early cognitive and linguistic skill interdependence.

How is communicative ability assessed in bilingual children with and without language impairment?add

The study's prototype screening tool utilizes a holistic model of communicative ability, evaluating linguistic, discourse, interactional, sociocultural, strategic, and monitoring skills (score distributions of TDB vs LIB). It emphasizes the need for varied assessments to prevent misdiagnosis.

> Master of Arts, 2006

Jolanta Garus Department of Curriculum, Teaching and Learning University of Toronto 

> Abstract

Studies examining biliteracy have concentrated predominantly on the positive contributions biliteracy makes in maintaining the first language. However, very few studies have examined how not achieving a high level of literacy in the community language (CL) affects the identity of adult, second generation immigrant Canadians. This study involved individuals from three different language groups including Cantonese, 

Polish and Urdu and examined whether their literacy abilities affect their perceptions of 

being bilingual. Through interviews and focus groups, insight was generated into these 

individuals’ definitions and perceptions of ethnicity, language and identity. The findings reveal that social, political and educational factors all play a role in the amount of CL literacy an individual has been exposed to. The majority of participants stated that a lack of biliteracy skills neither makes them feel less bilingual nor weakens strong ties to 

aspects of their ethnic identity.

“I would be surprised if you met anyone who is second generation who could read” (Sony, Urdu speaking participant). Chapter 1Background 

The purpose of this study is to examine the role community language (CL) 

literacy plays in shaping the identity of adult, second generation Canadians. Specifically, this study focuses on individuals who do not possess reading and writing ability in their community language’, and explores whether or not they still regard themselves as 

bilingual. 

My interest in this research topic is due in large part to my experiences growing up bilingual. I was born to Polish immigrant parents in a small British Columbia town and grew up speaking Polish to my parents and my brother. All my life I have been 

complimented at how clearly and fluently I speak Polish and as a result, I have always 

felt bilingual. As a teenager, I went through stages of accepting and rejecting my ethnic 

culture and identity. It was not until university that I discovered I had a bond with other students similar to myself, not specifically with Polish students, but more so with other 

second generation individuals. We shared stories of language barriers and cultural issues. No matter what our background, we seemed to share the same quality; we were all bilingual to one extent or another. This bilingual identity allowed me to claim both aCanadian and Polish identity which I have always appreciated. However, one aspect of my bilingualism has always plagued me - the fact that I cannot read and write in my community language. As I began my studies at the Ontario Institute for Studies in Education at the University of Toronto, I had no doubt that I would explore issues of identity and language maintenance. However, as I began to take classes that focused on issues of bilingualism                                      

> ! Community languages (CL) are languages spoken by members of minority groups or communities within amajority
> language context. For an explanation of why this term was chosen, please refer to the Terminology section located at
> the end of the Chapter 1.

and literacy, I quickly realized what a key role literacy plays in language maintenance and second language acquisition. The works of Jim Cummins, Lucy Tse, and Bernardo Ferdman inspired me to further investigate community language literacy. Cummins’ Common Underlying 

Proficiency (CUP) hypothesis (1981) made me recognize what an important role the first 

language plays in regards to learning a second. The CUP refers to the 

cognitive/academic proficiency that underlies academic performance in both languages. 

There is a great deal of research that supports this theory and the fact that “ESL readers used knowledge in their native language as they read in English. This supports the view that ‘native-language development can enhance ESL reading’” (Fitzgerald, 1995, p. 181 as cited in Cummins, 2001, p. 38-39). As well, first language literacy is vital in language maintenance and a positive social identity. Tse (2001) investigated how fully biliterate individuals managed to obtain a high degree of literacy in their heritage language. Factors ranged from participating in literacy environments and the participants having a high ethnolinguistic vitality. The former allowed the participants to see heritage language literacy as meaningful and important in a variety of contexts. The latter resulted from peer, parental and organizational support, which in turn helped to create a positive social identity in regards to their heritage language and culture. Ferdman (1990) too, found that literacy plays a key role in cultural identity. As literacy can be defined differently in each cultural group, and the process of becoming literate is implicated by social structures, a person’s cultural identity is defined by the literacy practices they engage in (Ferdman, 1990). If literacy “touches at our core in that it is the part of ourselves that connects with the social world around us” (Ferdman, 1990, p. 181), then what does this mean for people who lack an integral part of their language? Do the participants in this study feel disconnected from their first language and the 

community that maintains it? Or, do participants have a strong bilingual identity that 

embraces their community language? Research Questions The study involved nine second generation immigrants living in Toronto, Canada. Three participants were Cantonese speaking, three Polish speaking and three Urdu speaking. These individuals can all speak their CL very well, but have little or no ability 

to read and write in their respective languages. Through a variety of email lists, I

requested volunteers who met the criteria to join the study. After volunteers responded, I

administered a short questionnaire to confirm that participants were indeed second 

generation immigrants born in Canada or who came to Canada before the age of four, were fluent in their CL, did not have high level of literacy in their CL, had some post-secondary education and were between the ages of 19 and 35. After participants were randomly chosen, I conducted one or two semi-structured interviews with each of the nine participants and held one focus group with five of the nine individuals. These interviews enabled me to answer these research questions: 1) How do the participants perceive and define themselves in terms of belonging to an ethnic minority in Toronto, Canada? 2) Does a lack of community language literacy impact the participants’ sense of “being bilingual” and thus, in turn, their identity? 3) What factors help to explain why the participants have developed a high level of oral proficiency in their community language but have not been able to maintain ahigh level of literacy in their community language? 4) What advice would participants give to improve community language literacy in regards to educational and policy changes? Rationale Why Examine Biliteracy and Identity? Extensive attention has been given to first-language and second-language literacy development in English (see Cumming, 1998; Cummins, 1989, 1996; Barnard & Glynn,           

> 2003; Bialystok, 2001; Colombi &Schleppegrell, 2002; Olson and Torrance, 1991).

However, very little exists regarding the concept of biliteracy. Nancy Hornberger (1990) 

was one of the first to define this term as “any and all instances in which communication occurs in two (or more languages) in or around written material” (p. 213). This definition is problematic because it implies that two languages are being used at the same time. As a result, I prefer to use Reyes’ (2001) definition of biliteracy as: the mastery of the fundamentals of speaking, reading, and writing (knowing 

sound/symbol connections, conventions of print, accessing and conveying 

meaning through oral or print mode, etc.) in two linguistic systems. It also includes constructing meaning by making relevant cultural and linguistic connections with print and the learners’own lived experiences... as well as the interaction of the two linguistic systems to make meaning (Reyes, 2001, p. 98) Others who have studied biliteracy are Chevalier (2004), Farr (1994), McQuillan (1998), Perez (2004a, 2004b), Tse (2001) as well as Verhoeven and Durgunoglu (1998). However, all of these authors have focused on either those who are biliterate and how they became so, or on children learning two literacies in a bilingual classroom context. The socio-linguistic aspects of not achieving full community language literacy in regards to adult second generation Canadians has not yet been explored. More so, how this lack 

of literacy has impacted these individuals’ identity and views of their own bilingualism has yet to be investigated. A specific concentration on identity in literacy can be found, but most of the 

research focuses on immigrants (or their children) learning English literacy. Both 

Hoffman (1989) and Rodriguez (1982) give first hand accounts of how literacy learning in English created a conflict between their two cultures and thus, forced them to take on a

new identity. As well, studies of critical literacy, power relations and minority students             

> in schools are often cited while exploring identity and literacy (Cummins, 2001; Delpit,

1986). For instance, Delpit (1986) points out that schools exclude the kind of language and literacy that minority children bring from home because it does not contain the right kind of cultural capital for them to be successful, and thus impacts their identity.” Nevertheless, there is a gap in the research in regards to those who lack literacy in acommunity language. Very few studies examine how being fluent, but not literate, impacts these students’ education, relationships and their views of themselves.

Why Bilingualism? 

Other reasons for pursuing this area of research is to be able to probe further into the concepts of bilingual identity and who has the ‘right’ to claim one. The question of 

who is and who is not bilingual is more difficult to answer than it first appears. Baker and Prys Jones (1998, p. 2) suggest that in defining a bilingual person, we may wish to consider the following questions: e Should bilingualism be measured by how fluent a person is in two languages? e Should bilinguals only include people who have equal competence in both languages? e Is language proficiency the only criterion for assessing bilingualism, or should the use of two languages also be considered? e Most people would define a bilingual as a person who can speak two languages. What about a person who can understand a second language perfectly but cannot speak it? What about a person who can speak a language but is not literate in it? What about an individual who cannot speak or understand speech in a second language but can read and write in it? e Should self-perception and self-ascription be considered in defining who is bilingual? (as cited in Wei, 2000, p. 5) 

These questions are especially relevant when considering individuals who speak 

two languages and are much stronger in one language than another. While exploring the relevant research, I discovered there were no empirical studies that actually investigated individuals’ perceptions regarding who should be considered bilingual or not. By taking the time to delve into such questions, we can discover more about the very nature of 

bilingualism and the role of literacy. 

Participant Selection: Why Three Language Groups? The participants in my study come from three different language groups: Cantonese, Polish and Urdu. I chose these three groups for two different reasons. First, Iwanted to have a variety of languages and scripts in order to make the research more applicable to different language groups. Cantonese is a Sino-Tibetan language that uses 

single syllable characters, which may represent either a word, morpheme, or particle, and multi-syllabic words. Cantonese is identical to Mandarin in terms of writing because both languages use the same characters; however, pronunciation between the two languages is very different. On the other hand, Polish is written in a Latin alphabet, but uses diacritics such as kreska (graphically similar to acute accent), superior dot and ogonek. Urdu is an 

Indo-European language that is written right to left, and is a derivative of the Persian alphabet. As it goes beyond the scope of my study, I do not spend a great deal of time doing a comparative analysis of the three groups. However, differences and similarities 

are addressed throughout Chapters 4, 5 and 6. By investigating what kinds of community 

resources each language/cultural group maintains (for instance, community language classes, bookstores, community centers), we can get a better idea of why CL literacy was 

not obtained by the participants. Participant Selection: Why a Time of Arrival Continuum? The second reason for including Cantonese, Polish and Urdu speaking participants is related to when large numbers of each group immigrated to Canada. Several studies show the connection between ethnic group strength and language maintenance. For instance, a 1990 study examining the use of community languages in Canada stressed the centrality of the relative age of the linguistic group as a factor in determining whether first languages would be maintained, or whether the group would make a shift to the majority language. The proportion of new immigrants within the groups and the age structure of the group were also identified as significant predictors (Pendakur, 1990). As well, Jedwab (2000) concluded that heritage language knowledge 

and maintenance are dependent on time of arrival, length of residence in Canada, size of 

given community and degree of mixing between persons of different linguistic 

communities. 

A ‘high-voice’ cultural/language group is one that has access to an array of community resources (Gagné, 2004). One very important resource in terms of language           

> maintenance, and thus, the development of literacy and identity, is the

community/heritage language school. Pannu and Young’s study of 76 ethnic language schools in Canadian metropolitan cities pointed to the tremendous potential of these schools for the development of ethnic identity and literacy development (1980, p. 259). Terminology I have chosen to use the term, ‘community language’ when discussing the language spoken by members of minority groups or communities within a majority language context. ‘Community language’ is much more common in areas such as the United Kingdom and Australia. Other terms, such as ‘heritage language’, ‘minority language’ or ‘international language’ have also been used for similar definitions in other parts of the world. ‘Heritage language’ is probably the most commonly used term to 

describe languages other than the official language of a community. However, even 

though this term is still used extensively in the United States, it became controversial in the Canadian (especially in Ontario) context. Language classes for immigrant children 

held outside the regular school curriculum were originally titled ‘heritage language 

classes’. However, the term ‘heritage’ implies learning about past traditions rather than learning language skills that are important in a child’s academic and personal 

development (Cummins, 2005). Therefore in October 1993, a change in terminology occurred, 'Heritage Language’ became ‘International Languages' in order to do away with the negativity attached to the classes. The term ‘international language’ is a very broad term and can thus encompass ail languages learned, including those that are outside of aperson’s ethnic/cultural background; as a result, I have chosen not to use this term. 

Lastly, the term, ‘minority language’, can also be seen differently according to context. In one case, a minority language can be anything other than the official languages of Canada, English and French. However, a French family in Ontario might feel that they 

are far from being part of the majority in their area. As well, examining a language such as Cantonese, which is one of the largest language groups in the country, it might be 

difficult to call this a ‘minority language’ in the context of Toronto. Therefore, the term, ‘community language’ is most appropriate for this study and the context in which in takes place. However, in order to maintain academic integrity, when referring to other research I will use the term appropriated by the authors in their studies. Another term that will be used throughout this study is “second generation” Canadians. This term implies that a person was born in Canada to parents who were born outside of the country. Thus, immigrants arriving in Canada would be termed, “first generation” Canadians, whereas their Canadian born children are regarded as “second generation”. However, some of my participants may be also known as “generation 1.5” (Rumbaut & Ima, 1988). Generation 1.5 students are Canadian educated English 

language learners. There is great diversity among them in terms of their prior educational 

experience and native and English language proficiency. Some of these students 

immigrated to the Canada before or while they were in elementary school; others arrived 

during high school. Still others were born in this country but grew up speaking a

language other than English at home. One of the most common traits among generation 

1.5 students is limited or no literacy in the first language. According to Thonus (2003), 

many of these students “have lost or are in the process of losing their home languages 

without having learned their writing systems or academic registers. Unlike international 

students, generation 1.5 students lack a basis of comparison in fully developed oral, written, or both systems of a first language” (p. 18). Lastly, throughout the study, the terms ‘literacy’, ‘literacies’ and ‘biliteracy’ are used. The concept of literacy is very difficult to define for it can be seen from either acognitive or social perspective. I will go into greater detail surrounding the controversies around this term and others (i.e., ‘literacies’) in Chapter 2 of this thesis. Thus, for the sake of clarity, I will use Statistics Canada’s definition of literacy as “the ability of individuals to use printed and written information to function in society, reach their objectives, broaden their knowledge and increase their potential” (1996, para. 1). “Literacies” is a term used by Brian Street (among others) who views literacy as a social practice and cultural knowledge. The term ‘literacies’ therefore accounts for the fact that 

reading and writing can take on many forms, such as language and different cultural 

contexts of use. Lastly, the term biliteracy refers to the “mastery of the fundamentals of speaking, reading, and writing (knowing sound/symbol connections, conventions of print, accessing and conveying meaning through oral or print mode, etc.) in two linguistic systems” (Reyes, 2001, p. 98).  

> Theoretical Framework

Developing a theory around community language literacy and identity requires an examination of a number of interrelated factors. I have approached this by examining competing discourses and the theoretical construct of literacy, identity, and language maintenance. Although I am investigating individuals who do not possess the technical skill of reading and writing in their community language, my analysis of the literature 

surrounding literacy and identity shows that literacy cannot be viewed as simply the inability to read and write. Social structures and power relations play a critical role in challenging common assumptions about community language literacy. As a result, I will use Reder’s 1994 Practice Engagement Theory as my guiding framework. However, I do not disregard other discourses and perspectives on literacy because these help to                

> understand why the participants have not been able to develop or maintain ahigh level of

literacy in their community language literacy and how this impacts on their identity.               

> Practice Engagement Theory Reder (1994) argues that literacy development is determined by the qualities of an

individual’s engagement in particular literacy practices. Factors that affect such             

> engagement, i.e., whether or not achild (the participant) receives bedtime stories (the

literacy practice), or whether heritage language classes are available, will facilitate or hinder reading and writing acquisition (p. 48). Thus, Practice Engagement Theory deals               

> with what “it is about aset of engagements that produces or fails to produce literacy

development” (Reder, 1994, p. 50). This approach is relevant to placing literacy development within the cross-cultural framework because “it brings into focus the issues of cultural and linguistic differences in the occurrence of particular literacy practices as              

> well as in the qualities of individuals’ engagement in those practices” (1994, p. 49).

Thus, by focusing on how my participants have different definitions and perceptions of           

> their two literacies (English and community language) and by exploring their

participation (or lack of it) in these literacy practices, it has helped me uncover how different literacy practices have helped or hindered their biliteracy abilities.                                                                 

> It is important to note that the Practice Engagement Theory does not place any special emphasis on formal literacy instruction. In fact, instruction is seen as equal to that of other literacy practices which may take place either in the home or in other community contexts. As well, the theory considers that learning occurs when learners engage with a demonstration (“opportunities to see how something is done”) and, in so

doing, assimilate the demonstration of another and transform it into actions of their own 10                

> (Smith, 1983 as quoted from Reder, 1994, p. 50). In addition, Smith also argues that in

order for learners to be fully engaged, there must also be an absence of expectations that 

learning will be difficult or will not occur. Therefore, if students are led to believe that 

learning will be difficult, boring or impossible, this will block engagement and thus 

learning (1994, p. 51). As a result, I investigate if demonstrations either in the home or in 

an educational setting led the participants to think that reading and writing in their 

community language was difficult, not worth the effort to learn or impossible to master. 

The concept of biliteracy cannot be seen as static as many bilinguals are stronger in one language than another. For instance, when individuals are interacting with the 

written word in their stronger language, they may more likely see themselves as experts, 

and fluent in this domain. However, if individuals attempt to read in their weaker 

language, they may perceive themselves very differently. In this case, there could be afeeling of frustration at a sense of being ‘illiterate’ and unable to decode a specific text. 

As a result, a more flexible approach is needed to define literacy. Practice Engagement 

Theory states that people may engage with three different types of literacy aspects: technological, functional, and social and argues that people may engage with any or all of these three aspects in various and unmatched ways. Technological engagement accounts for directly manipulating written materials, or in other words, actually comprehending the script and the relationship between units or phonemes, i.e., performing the task of reading and writing. Functional engagement refers to an individual not being personally involved in the reading and writing, but allows that person to interact closely with someone else to carry out the task. These individuals may have “specialized knowledge and expertise” in order to help others who are engaged technologically. Therefore, functional knowledge about a literary practice refers to knowledge of how the technology is used for specific purposes. Being socially engaged is to be neither technologically nor functionally engaged in the literary practices, but to have knowledge of the practice and its repercussions on the life of the community. 

These individuals must regularly take other’s technological and functional engagement 

into account (Reder, 1987, p. 257). For instance, a minority child in a majority school setting can often acquire a negative social meaning of school-based literacy because their own “home literacy” is not appreciated or acknowledged in the classroom; therefore, 11 

making it difficult for that child to become technologically or functionally engaged. Dei 

(1997) for instance, concludes that a curriculum which disregards the African component in Canadian history and society lacks personal relevance and I believe, portrays anegative social meaning for the African students within these classrooms. In regards to 

my own research, adopting this framework enables me to question participants’ literacy in terms of not only decoding the written word, but also whether or not they understand the social meanings behind the words they cannot comprehend. 

Becoming literate involves engagement at various levels as described in Reder’s 

framework (1994, p. 54). Therefore, if a person has unequal access to participatory roles 

and modes of engagement in literacy practices, this may result in parallel inequalities of socialization and development. Reder (1994) argues that when technological knowledge develops before functional, such as is often the case in Western schooling which frequently uses a decontextualized pedagogy of literacy, this can cause difficulties for the students. Olson (1977), Cook-Gumperz and Gumperz (1981), and Snow (1983) suggested that this “context independence” makes literacy development problematic for some students (Reder, 1994, p. 55). Six of the nine participants in this study took part in 

international/heritage language classes during their childhood years. Within these 

classes, some teaching of reading and writing did take place, yet the students never reached a high level of literacy. Thus, it is important to investigate what kind of literacy experiences these students had in and out of the classroom. Reder’s (1994) theory has been used in a variety of contexts. Smith and Sheehan (1998) used the Practice Engagement Theory to help analyze different adult ethnic and racial groups’ reading practices and proficiencies in regards to the National Adult Literacy Survey in the United States. As well, Hamilton (2002) uses Reder’s theory to allow for a more fluid characterization of literacy in her chapter, Supporting lifelong learning: Perspectives on learning. She argues that literacy can be interpreted in many different ways with a person moving “in and out of being learners in different roles”, with notions of exchange and identity strongly linked (Hamilton, 2002, p. 183). Therefore, Reder’s ideas contribute well to her own work. Nevertheless, throughout my research, Ihave been unable to find the Practice Engagement Theory linked to any major empirical study or to biliteracy. Thus, my thesis will fill in this gap by providing a research piece 12                            

> that uses this theory to examine community language literacy practices of second generation immigrant Canadians. As aresult of its focus on how individuals interact with avariety of social

meanings and choices they make regarding development and use of literacy, the Practice Engagement Theory provides a framework that can be effective in examining the development and use of literacy in multicultural societies.
