> Literature Review

Identity is a multifaceted concept which has been studied through various theoretical paradigms. The concept can be seen as not only fixed (Chambers, 1991; Van den Berghe, 1987) or fluid, but also either innate or socially constructed (Bhabha, 1998; 

Gérin-Lajoie, 2003; Hall, 1990). A person’s identity is linked to a variety of aspects including: gender, ethnicity, language, religion, family, and friends. In this study, I focus on the impact of language and literacy on a person’s identity. 

In preparing this literature review, I explored research related to a number of areas including community/heritage language, language maintenance, bilingualism, first and second language literacy, language learning and of course, the role of each of the 

preceding in shaping identity. As I have discovered no major research focusing on the lack of community language literacy and its impact on identity, I have arranged my literature review into two major parts. The first part focuses on identity and particularly 

on how identity is socially constructed and the role that language plays in this process. Next I explore how ethnicity impacts on identity. The relationship between language 

maintenance and its effects on identity are also described. Last, bilingual and bicultural identities are addressed. The second part of this review focuses on literacy and biliteracy 

in terms of the community language. Definitions of literacy are provided and a socio-cultural approach to literacy is described. The challenges involved in achieving and maintaining biliteracy as well as the various routes that lead to biliteracy are described. Finally, I discuss the research that relates a person’s literacy abilities to their identity. Identity Language and Identity Some view language simply as a communication tool. However, it is much more than that — language is used when we think, feel, and experience the world around us. These experiences and the way we choose to express them, formulates who we are as            

> individuals, and in turn our identity. Le Page and Tabouret-Keller, in their

13 14 groundbreaking ethnographic work studying Creole-speaking Caribbean individuals, 

stated that language is the “focal centre of our acts of identity” (1985, p. 248) and “the means by which individuals both identify themselves and identify with others” (1985, p. 

5). Eva Hoffman’s autobiography, “Lost in Translation” (1991) offers a first hand account of how as a young immigrant from Poland, she struggled to redefine her identity in a new country and language. In an interview with Harry Kreisler, Hoffman states, 

“language is not only something that we use instrumentally, but it is something that truly shapes us, and that truly shapes our perceptions of the world...” (2000, para. 4). Asa 

result, language can be seen as a “powerful socializing medium” (Schieffelin & Ochs, 1986, p. 172) implicated in not only identity, but also in “relationships, culture, and aspirations, and transmitting information about events, activities, affective domain, tone, 

mood, the organization of society, the current state of ‘knowledge’, the means to question              

> and evaluate that knowledge, and all other aspects of the social world” (Kouritzin, 1999,

p. 15). Identity as Fluid and Socially Constructed Language and identity have been combined in a variety of theoretical frameworks. 

Those working within variationist sociolinguistics (Labov, 1966) see identity tied to broad social structures and believe that language difference is based on the assumption 

that “for the most part people sound the way you would expect them to sound given the 

facts about their class, sex, age, and region” (Chambers, 2003; p. 115). Thus, a person 

simply expresses their one, never changing identity. Over the past fifteen years, scholars such as Cameron (1990), Tannen (1993), and Williams (1995) have criticized this view for considering identity simply as an explanatory concept as well as for seeing language 

as fixed, rather than fluid and purposefully set out by individual speakers (Blackledge &

Pavlenko, 2001, p. 244). These researchers argue that multiple identities are constructed 

and negotiated through different forms of language use, and therefore, cannot be seen as            

> static or uni-dimentional. Several more recent studies (Bucholtz &Hall, 2005; Giampapa,

2001, 2004; Heller, 1999) demonstrated that on many occasions people do not at all sound the way one would expect them to given their class, sex, age and religion. For 

instance, Giampapa (2004) argues that there is a “norm setting dictating who is in and 15 who is out” in the Italian-Canadian community (p. 194). The criteria of exclusion include areas such as: linguistic repertoire, religion, and sexual orientation. In regards to religion, “being Italian Canadian and Catholic is the norm”; for linguistic repertoire, 

‘standard’ Italian is best; and for sexual orientation, heterosexuality is the dominant discourse. However, Giampapa’s participants go against one or all of these ‘standards’, being either: gay, evangelical, and speaking a dialect of Italian. As a result, scholars have 

had to focus more of their research on the basis of identity being “an emergent product rather than the pre-existing source of linguistic...practices and therefore as fundamentally a social and cultural phenomenon” (Bucholtz & Hall, 2005, p. 588). Some of the earlier works that view identity as fluid and constructed in social 

interaction came from an ethnographically oriented interactional sociolinguistic 

standpoint. Gumperz’ (1982) study on language and social identity and LePage and Tabouret-Keller’s (1985) research on language use in the Caribbean gave this theory avoice in the area of identity (Pavlenko & Blackledge, 2004, p. 8). LePage and Tabouret-

Keller (1985) argue that individuals themselves create their own models of language that either mirror the behaviour of the groups they want to be associated with, or diverge with 

the behaviour of those groups from which they want to be dissociated. Gumperz’ edited 

book, Language and Social Identity (1982) pushed forward the research on language and identity, but most of the authors support the view that the linguistic system is something 

imposed on its speakers, who are its passive users. Gumperz’ book begins by claiming that: We seek to develop interpretive sociolinguistic approaches to human interaction which account for the role that communicative phenomena play in the exercise of power and control and in the production and reproduction of social identity. Our basic premise is that social processes are symbolic processes but that symbols have meaning only in relation to the forces which control the utilization and allocation of environmental resources (Gumperz & Cook-Gumperz, 1982, p. 1). According to John Joseph, this leaves no space for individuals to interpret, project and ‘perform’ symbolic meaning (Joseph, 2004, p. 78). Other critics of the interactional sociolinguistic approach criticize the mandatory links between languages and specific national or regional groups which hide the fact that individuals may also construct particular identities through linguistic resources of groups to which they don’t belong (Cutler, 1999 as quoted from Blackledge and Pavlenko, 2001, p. 244). For instance, 16 Rampton’s (1995) work explores the nature of “language crossing”, by which individuals take up out-group minority languages present in the community as a means of demonstrating anti-racism and establishing alternative identities. Consequently, alanguage affiliation can often times have little to do with nationality. Due to the efforts of researchers such as Gal (1989), Heller (1999) and Woolard 

(1998) the concept of identity began to be viewed within larger social, political, 

economic and cultural systems. The poststructuralist approach views identity not as static 

and one-dimensional, but as multiple, changing, and a site of struggle, constructed in 

linguistic interaction (Bhabha, 1990; Bourdieu, 1991; Le Page & Tabouret Keller, 1985; Norton Pierce, 1995; 2000; Rosenthal & Hrynevich, 1985). Therefore research in this realm according to Blackledge and Pavlenko favors a far more fluid approach in which individuals are seen to “cross” between different ethnic groups, and an individual’s 

identities are seen to be “multiple, dynamic, and subject to change” (2001, p. 249). One 

of the first scholars to explore identity in this way was Bourdieu (1991) and his view of 

language as a form of cultural capital. 

Bourdieu (1977; 1991), a French sociologist, produced a great deal of work that focused on the relationship between language, identity and symbolic power through the concepts of habitus and cultural and linguistic capital. The habitus is a set of dispositions people possess that direct “ways of being” or in other words, how they will act and speak (Bourdieu, 1991, p. 17). Through our lived experiences our habitus is constantly being reconstructed through influences from the dominant culture and eventually becomes anatural part of ourselves. As a result, for Bourdieu, individual identity is not aprecondition of social action, but rather arises from it. The problem with this notion of habitus is that it is very rigid and speculates that individuals do not have any choice in deciding when to speak a certain way, with whom, and where. Gee (1996; 2002) extends Bourdieu’s theory by exploring the idea of “Discourses”. Local “discourses”, with a small d, are “connected stretches of language that make sense, like conversations [or] stories” (1996, p. 127). Through these “discourses”, individuals begin to recognize and take on a variety of identities: i.e., astudent, mother, wife, daughter, sister, Canadian, etc. By taking part in “discourse”, 17 

individuals express their “ways of being and doing” or ‘big D’ “Discourses”. These “Discourses” allow people to enact and/or recognize a specific and distinctive socially situated identity (Gee, 2002, p. 159-160). Therefore, for bilinguals, how they choose to use language and literacy defines how they are “being-doing” as either an Urdu speaking Muslim or a Polish-Canadian person. Giampapa (2004) also argues, “ethnicity and 

language are the entry points in understanding the participants’ identity narratives. These are the claims to identities, positions, and spaces within their worlds. Articulating what it 

means ‘to be and become Italian-Canadian’ reflects their range of identity positions and 

negotiability of identities” (Giampapa, 2004, p. 200). Cultural and linguistic capital are a part of the habitus and contribute to how aperson will act or speak in a particular situation. This capital is determined by one’s 

social position and factors such as race, ethnicity, class and gender. Everyone has cultural and linguistic capital; however, the capital that some members of society possess is not always seen as the ‘correct’ capital (Bourdieu, 1991). People who do not use the cultural and linguistic capital of the dominant group will therefore experience hardships in school, work, and society in general. When cultural and linguistic capital is not valued, self-confidence and identity suffer and the students will often become silenced within the 

school and later in society. Norton (2000) illustrates how the identity of the immigrant 

women in her study was shaped by the fact that they did not possess the right cultural 

capital in terms of accent and knowledge of English. Consequently, the identity placed on them by the target language speakers had an influence on how the participants defined 

> themselves.

The previous sections discussed research surrounding language and identity in regards to different theoretical frameworks, and identity as a fluid construct that is constantly being negotiated by the individual. In the next section, I focus on ethnic identity and how language is involved in its construction. Language and Ethnic Identity There is a widely believed assumption that there is a connection between the language spoken by members of an ethnic group and group members’ identity. Language is crucial because of its role as “the recorder of paternity, the expresser of patrimony, and 18 

the carrier of phenomenology” (Fishman, 1989, p. 32). In other words, language is what keeps us connected to our ancestors by maintaining and expressing certain cultural behaviours and values, and all the while allowing us to express what and why we have those attachments and behaviours. The first area to explore the connection between language and ethnic identity was the socio-psychological approach, which has attempted 

to theorize identity, negotiation of identity and language contact outcomes. Some of the 

first researchers to do work within this paradigm were Tajfel (1974), Giles and Byrne 

(1982) and Giles and Johnson (1987). Tajfel examined the ethnic component of social 

identity and defined it as “that part of an individual’s self-concept which derives from his knowledge of his membership of a social group (or groups) together with the value and emotional significance attached to that membership” (1974, p. 69). Building from this framework, the Ethnolinguistic Identity Theory (Giles and Byrne, 1982) considered language to be a significant marker of ethnic identity. Giles and his colleagues focused on ethnolinguistic vitality and language choice and thus, came up with the concepts of ‘divergence’ and ‘convergence’. The former describes that when individuals have apositive ethnic group identity, they will automatically and additionally have a positive social identity. Consequently, they will make use of the in-group language by adopting strategies such as accentuated speech styles and perhaps achieve a low level of second language proficiency. On the other hand, ‘convergence’ describes a situation in which 

individuals have negative attitudes toward an in-group language. As a result, they will 

acquire a negative social identity and therefore try to assimilate with the out-group by identifying themselves with speakers of the dominant language. This theory later 

influenced researchers such as Clément and Noels (1992) who suggest that linguistic minority members will often choose to identify with a group that has the highest ethnolinguistic vitality, therefore contributing the most to a positive social identity. 

Blackledge and Pavlenko (2001) question this theory by asking: a) What about individuals who have a positive ethnic group identity, but still attempt to assimilate with the dominant group, or in-group members who have a negative ethnic in-group identity but demonstrate hostility toward the out-group? b) How about individuals who have more than one in-group? Thus, even though Giles and Bye did open up the idea of 

connecting language and ethnic identity, their theory contains very rigid categories in 19 which multiple, negotiated, and socially constructed identities simply cannot fit (2001, p. 

4). Another criticism of the socio-psychological approach is that it does not take into 

account bilingual and multilingual individuals who may be members of multiple communities (Blackledge and Pavlenko, 2001, p. 244-245). As a result, more recent 

researchers such as Nagel (1994) and Giampapa (2004) see ethnicity as negotiated and 

socially constructed. Giampapa, in discussing her Italian-Canadian participants’ issues with identity, argues that, “language plays a salient and defining role in the way these participants desire to be positioned and position themselves (Giampapa, 2004, p. 200-201). Nagel describes that “individuals and groups create and recreate their personal and collective histories, the membership boundaries of their group, and the content and 

meaning of their ethnicity” (Nagel, 1994, p. 102). Ethnicity, according to the author, consists of two basic building blocks: ethnic identity and culture. Ethnic identity pertains to the psychological processes involved in defining group memberships, while culture 

forms the perceived basis for those definitions. 

Specifically focusing on ethnic identity, Wsevolod Isajiw (1997) has been aprominent researcher within the field of ethnicity and no review of the literature regarding this topic would be complete without him. He defines identity as “‘...the manner in which persons locate themselves psychologically in relation to one or more social systems, and the way in which they perceive others as locating them in relation to those systems” (1997, p. 90). Isajiw distinguishes between external and internal aspects of ethnic identity. External aspects refer to observable behaviour, both cultural and social, such as (1) speaking an ethnic language, practicing ethnic traditions, (2) participation in ethnic personal networks, such as family and friendships, (3) participation in ethnic institutional organizations, such as churches, schools, enterprises, media, (4) participation in ethnic voluntary associations, such as clubs, ‘societies,’ youth organizations and (5) 

participation in functions sponsored by ethnic organizations such as picnics, concerts, 

public lectures, rallies, dances. The internal aspects of ethnic identity refer to images, ideas, attitudes, and feelings which are interconnected with the external behaviour (Isajiw, 1993, p. 8). These two aspects of ethnic identity are not dependent upon each other and may often vary independently. For example, a second generation Canadian 20 may feel strongly connected to their ethnicity, but may not speak the language associated   

> with that culture.

Other researchers (Phinney and Tarver 1988; Phinney 1989; Tse, 1998; 1999; 2000) argue that ethnic identity is a developmental process, in which the individual goes through a variety of stages that include complete rejection of the group to actively 

integrating the ethnic culture in their lives. Tse (1998) examined the autobiographies of 

39 Asian-Americans and produced four stages of ethnic identity development. In stage 1, (“Unawareness”) individuals are unconscious of their minority status and/or the subordinate status that goes with it. This stage is relatively short and usually occurs before entering school or leaving the ethnic enclave. Stage 2 (“Ethnic Ambivalence/Evasion”) has minority group members desire to integrate into the target culture, as a result, there is a sense of apathy toward or even rejection of the heritage culture and language. Typically, this stage occurs during childhood and adolescence, and may extend into adulthood. Those in this stage have little interest in the heritage language, and may even avoid using it. For example one of her participants, Maria Shao gave an account of how her knowledge of Chinese brought her a sense of embarrassment when she was in elementary school, “if I had friends over, I purposely spoke English to my parents. Normally, we only spoke Chinese at home. Because of the presence of a non-Chinese, I used to purposely speak English’” (Tse, 1998, p. 21). The third stage (“Emergence”) is when many people rediscover their ethnic heritage after dealing with the fact that they are part of an ethnic minority group. For some, it may lead to accepting 

the minority heritage over the majority group. At this stage, it is common that 

individuals will connect and form strong friendships with others from the same ethnic or racial group (See Zeon & Garcia-Vaquez, 1995; Zweigenhaft & Domhoff, 1991). Lastly, in the fourth stage (“Ethnic Identity Incorporation”) minority group members begin to accept themselves and settle many of the ethnic identity issues that came up previously and join the “ethnic minority American group” (e.g. Mexican-Americans) (Tse, 1998, p. 15-16). Tse herself admits there are some limitations to this model, for instance not all minority group members may go through this developmental model, especially those who have grown up in a strong ethnic enclave. In addition, not all stages have to be gone through and it is quite possible that identity development does not stop at stage 4 (Tse, 2] 1998, p. 16-17). Indeed, a person’s ethnic identity can evolve and go back and forth in 

between stages, suggesting a fluid and ever changing notion of identity. As has been defined by the sections above, language plays an integral part in aperson’s identity, especially in terms of ethnicity. However, in order to truly understand the ties between language and identity, we must examine why and how people lose or maintain their heritage language and how this maintenance/shift impacts identity. Identity and Language Maintenance 

As more and more people move around the globe, finding new homes in new countries with new languages, the topic of language maintenance and loss has become 

increasingly salient in today’s world. In the North American context, especially, this area has been researched extensively because of its importance to immigrant families 

struggling to keep their language and culture alive. 

Fishman (1991) argued that both language and cultural shift result in “losing sight of one’s true self, the security that self brings, the cultural heritage it fosters, and the value it has for one’s life as well as the lives of others” (as quoted from Withers, 2004, p. 426). Researchers (e.g. Arnberg, 1987; Hakuta & D’ Andrea, 1992; Wong Fillmore, 1991) have correlated such things as parental education, attitude, and first language literacy, elapsed time since immigration, first language status, diglossia’, literacy, age, family size, types of daycare and schooling, and other related variables to language loss (Kouritzin, 1999, p. 15). Scholars have also found that with language shift comes a loss 

of familial communication and regret on the part of the individual (Tannenbaum &

Howie, 2002). Nevertheless, according to Krashen (1998), heritage languages are extremely difficult to maintain, especially in the cases of second generation immigrants. Feuerverger argues that maintaining a language and cultural lifestyle is often easier for first generation immigrants because they can remain within their ethnic enclaves, engaging in little or no interaction with the majority cultures (1989, p. 50-51). Their children, however, “live in a bicultural setting - they are immersed in the culture of their home (through parents and relatives) and are brought into contact with the culture of the                          

> 3Originally defined by Ferguson (1959), the definition of diglossia was expanded in the work of Fishman (1967) to encompass all situations of functional differentiation between language varieties.

22 wider society by way of the school systems and the media. Thus, it is not difficult to 

understand how easily second generation children may begin to experience psychological conflict as they perceive themselves caught between two cultures with their competing 

values” (Feuerverger, 1989, p. 51). As a result, the vitality of the ethnocultural group may be affected and, as a consequence, motivation for language maintenance may decrease. 

Therefore, Feuerverger found that the greater the attempt at maintaining the first 

language, the stronger the cultural identity of her participants, thereby increasing the enthnolinguistic vitality of the ethnic group (1989, p. 64). Other studies have found a variety of reasons for language maintenance. Having 

friends from the same ethnic background also plays a strong role in language maintenance because it gives individuals another strong domain to use the language in (the concept of ‘domain’ will be discussed in the next section) (Clyne & Kipp, 1999; Luo & Wiseman, 2000; Schechter & Bayley, 2003). Smolicz (2002) maintains that core values, which are regarded as forming the most fundamental components of a group’s culture and membership, play a role in language maintenance. For some ethnic groups (South Asian particularly), family life and culture is most important (Faria, 2001). For other groups, such as the Chinese, Polish and Greek communities, language is a strong core value, therefore more likely to be maintained (Smolicz, 2002). Lee (2002) also found that frequency of visits to Korea had a positive effect on the level of Korean proficiency among second generation immigrants to the United States. In addition, seventy percent of her participants mentioned that “they needed to be 

taught about the benefits and usefulness of learning Korean instead of being just forced to 

learn it because ‘it is your parents’ language’” (Lee, 2002, p. 122). Such knowledge can therefore lead to positive attitudes towards the language, a motivation to learn (Baker, 

1992) as well as a desire to invest in the language, thus improving one’s social (and in the case of the participants — ethnic) identity (Norton Peirce, 1995). In terms of identity, she 

discovered that the group that was more proficient in Korean associated themselves with Koreans or Korean-Americans (Lee, 2002, p. 125). Therefore, Lee claims, they are more successful in balancing their two cultures and tend to classify themselves as bicultural. Similar findings emerged from Cho’s (2001) study where participants who developed their heritage language had a strong ethnic identity and greater interactions with heritage 23 language speakers. As a result, as Cummins (1981) mentions in his earlier work, learning a heritage language - particularly to a high level of proficiency - may promote the group cohesion necessary for ethnic identity maintenance. 

The research presented in the prior section discusses the factors that lead to 

language loss and maintenance in regards to heritage languages. Much of the research 

points to the fact that the more fluent individuals are in their heritage language, the more closely they identify with their ethnic group. However, it is clear that the majority language can have an effect on the lives of second generation immigrants, thus possibly 

creating a bicultural and/or bilingual identity. As a result, the research in the next section deals with this topic. Bilingualism Before I can speak to the literature on bilingual identity, I believe that it appropriate to spend some time discussing the area of bilingualism itself. As mentioned in Chapter 1, there are many questions surrounding how to define bilingualism. These questions permeate almost every beginning chapter of works dealing with this topic (see Baker, 2006; Bialystock, 2001; Shin, 2005; Wei, 2000). The difficulty for researchers in 

defining bilingualism is that there are many different circumstances and environments where acquiring another language takes place. 

Most research points to the fact that bilinguals are rarely equally proficient in both languages. Romaine (1995) argues that the idea of balanced bilingualism “is a mythical one, an artifact of a theoretical perspective that takes the monolingual speaker as its point of reference” (as quoted from Shin, 2005, p. 16). Many scholars have revealed that contexts of use, or domains, are one reason why bilinguals may be stronger in one language than another. The concept of public and private spheres is taken from Fishman’s (1965; 1972) theory of linguistic domains, in which language choice in abilingual community varies from domain to domain and the use of one language is seen as more appropriate than another depending on certain factors (Hudson, 1989). These domains are envisaged as “congruent combinations of a particular kind of speaker and addressee, in a particular kind of place, talking about a particular kind of topic” (Hudson 1989, p. 80). Often the first language, or community language is only used in situations 24 

within the private domain, which consists of the home environment, i.e., between family members, and in intimate interactions. On the other hand the second language, or in many cases English, is used predominantly in the public domain, or the language of greater society, i.e., school, work, and friends. This finding appears across a variety of language groups (Fishman, 1991; Hakuta & D’Andrea, 1992) applying both to the use of |language and to attitudes towards it (as cited in Tannenbaum, 2003, p. 375). Bilingual Identity and Language As previously mentioned the ties between ethnicity and identity are very strong. However, if a person grows up in between two cultures, one of the home, and one of the dominant society, it becomes difficult to choose either one or the other culture to identify with. As a result, much current research depicts a bilingual and/or bicultural identity which many children of immigrants can more comfortably relate to. According to Kanno (2003) studying bilingual and bicultural identity is how “bilingual individuals position themselves between two languages and two (or more) cultures, and how they incorporate these languages and cultures into their sense of who they are” (Kanno, 2003, p. 3). Thus, by integrating both languages and cultures, an individual does not necessarily have to choose between one culture and another, but instead finds a space to call their own. Bhabha calls this a “third space” and ties it into aconcept called hybridity. For Bhabba (1998) hybridity is a state within which the subject constructs a renegotiated space set from the borders of exclusion, which is neither assimilation nor collaboration. He argues that hybrid identities “deploy the partial culture 

from which they emerge to construct visions of community, and versions of historic memory, that give narrative form to the minority positions they occupy: the outside of 

the inside: the part is the whole” (Bhabha, 1998, p. 34). Stuart Hall also explores the 

concept of hybridity and argues that identities are “constantly producing and reproducing          

> themselves anew, through transformation and difference” (Hall, 1994, p. 402).

A considerable amount of research argues that bilingual and bicultural individuals therefore, integrate their two ethnicities without having to disregard one or the other, especially in the cases of second generation immigrants (Hall, 1994; LaFramboise, Coleman, and Gerton, 1993; Jones Diaz, 1998; Kanno, 2003; Kim, 1992; Maira, 2002; 25 

Morales, 2002; Sudrez-Orozco, 2002). LaFramboise and his colleagues (1993) insist that, “a vital step in the development of an effective partnership among minorities and the 

majority group involves moving away from the assumptions of the linear model of 

cultural acquisition to a clearer understanding of the process of developing cultural 

competence as a two way street” (LaFramboise, Coleman, and Gerton , 1993, p. 409.). 

This “two way street” allows a sense of belonging in two cultures without jeopardizing aperson’s cultural/ethnic identity. Ed Morales uses the term “Spanglish” to describe the bilingual/bicultural state in of Latinos living in the United States. “The root of Spanglish is a very universal state of being. It is displacement from one place, home, to another place, home, in which one feels at home in both places, yet at home in neither place. . .Spanglish is the state of belonging to at least two identities at the same time, and not 

being confused or hurt by it” (Morales 2002, p. 7-8). Kanno (2003), in her narrative 

study of Japanese students who spent their teenage years in North America and then returned to Japan for university, views bilingualism and biculturalism through a

“multicompetence” lens (Cook, 1992; 1999) which sees a bilingual person’s cultures and languages as a whole “rather than separating out each language and culture as if ‘the 

bilingual is (or should be) two monolinguals in one person’ (Grosjean, 1992, p. 52)” (Kanno, 2003, p. 7). Carola Suarez-Orozco (2002), takes a slightly different approach in her chapter, Formulating Identity in a Globalized World, and considers the notion of transcultural identities. She asserts that children of immigrants have to “creatively fuse 

aspects of two or more cultures - the parental tradition and the new culture or cultures. In so doing, they synthesize an identity that does not require them to choose between cultures, but rather allows them to develop an identity that incorporates traits of both             

> cultures all the while fusing additive elements (Falicov, 2002 as cited in Suarez-Orozco,

2002, p. 192). 

Despite all of the research pointing toward a unified identity that fuses together both languages and cultures, we cannot disregard the fact that quite often these bilingual/biculutural individuals are forced to negotiate between their identities 

depending on the context and motivations of the speaker and listener. 

Bicultural/bilingual individuals may find identity negotiation complicated because of “the either/or terms imposed on them by the dominant discourses of language and identity” 26 

(Pavlenko, 2004, p. 340). Giampapa (2001) discovers that Salvatore, one of her Italian-Canadian participants is “performing a balancing act” by using English, standard Italian and an Italian dialect in different situations. In one “very awkward situation” he 

describes his frustration when he was positioned in a group of people that all spoke and 

expected him to speak one of his three different languages. As a result, because of 

constant negotiation and construction, bilingual and bicultural identities can bring about 

conflict in terms of having to live in between two cultures and languages. However important the tie seems to be in regards to language and bilingual identity, some research does point to the fact that knowledge of a language does not necessarily equal knowledge of a culture. Hoffman (1991) sees bilingualism and biculturalism to exist in varying degrees along the continuum (as quoted from Lee, 2002, p. 119). For instance, many second generation immigrants may have a good knowledge of their parents’ culture, but may speak very little of the language. Gérin-Lajoie (2003), 

in her ethnographic study on identity construction in Ontario, explores two francophone 

high school students and how they both claim to be bilingual, but perceive it very differently. One student values the importance of the language and culture, and thus claims a francophone identity, while the other student sees language as simply a method 

of communication, resulting in a disassociation with the francophone culture. 

The research presented in the previous section shows how bilingual and/or 

bicultural identity is a complex phenomenon. Biculturalism, as we have seen, can often 

lead to bilingualism, but it is not always that bilingualism leads to biculturalism. As mentioned, Morales (2002) found that Latino-Americans who grew up in both cultures, were in most cases bilingual. On the other hand, Gérin-Lajoie (2003) shows individuals who can speak both French and English very well, but only some choose to have an 

affiliation with both cultures. As well, despite a great deal of research that suggests that a

state of hybridity forms and that a bilingual identity does not force an individual to choose one language/culture over the other, there is proof that in some cases, people do indeed have to choose one language and perhaps, one identity over the other. The next section examines a very a significant part of language: literacy. I will discuss literacy and illiteracy in terms of definitions and different approaches, focusing specifically on 

the sociocultural approach. 27 

Literacy Literacy(ies): Definition(s) 

Literacy is a term difficult to define, yet its importance in the human world is 

undoubtable. The concept of literacy has been explored through many different 

perspectives: psycholinguistic (Adams, 1990; Smith, 1994; Stanovich, 1992); 

sociocultural (Gee, 1996; 2002; Vygotsky, 1978); and critical theory (Freire, 1970; Macedo, 1994). Some of these researchers (psycholinguistic) view literacy as a cognitive function in which one is able to examine words on a page and decode the information into words that make up sentences. On the other hand, there are those who see literacy from a social point of view (socio-cultural), where it is influenced by social functions and power dynamics (critical). It can be argued that those who have little or no ability to read and write may be classified as “illiterate”. According to the United Nations, illiteracy is defined as “the inability to read and write a simple message in any language” (United Nations, 2005, Technical Notes section, para. 1). As well, according to the cognitive or psycholinguistic model, literacy is seen as an identifiable set of skills or a tool that once a

person obtains, they are able to classify themselves as ‘literate’. Literacy, as defined by 

Statistics Canada, is “the ability of individuals to use printed and written information to function in society, reach their objectives, broaden their knowledge and increase their 

potential” (1996, para. 1). Assuming that literacy in itself will have effects on other social and cognitive practices, without exploring the social and economic circumstances 

that added or caused a person’s “illiteracy” is what Street refers to as the autonomous model of literacy (1984). On the other hand, the ideological model of literacy sees 

literacy as a social practice and cultural knowledge: “the ways in which people address 

reading and writing are themselves rooted in conceptions of knowledge, identity, and being” (Street, 2003). Street is just one of the major researchers who has adopted asocio-cultural approach to study literacy and ‘literacies’. The plural form accounts for the fact that reading and writing can take on many forms, such as language and different cultural contexts of use. As a result, a socio-cultural approach is appropriate to investigate aspects of community language literacy and identity. 28 Sociocultural Approach 

The socio-cultural approach has gained increasing popularity as a paradigm in 

which to study literacy (for examples, see Barton and Hamilton, 1998; 2000; Gee, 1996; Heath, 1983; Moll; 1994; Street, 1984; 1991; 2003). Using a socio-cultural framework, Moll (1994) defines literacy in cultural terms and views children as becoming literate 

within the cultures of their communities and their families. This theory derived from 

Vygotsky (1998) who emphasized the social world where learning and literacy emerge. 

As a result, researchers within the socio-cultural realm focus on the cultural meanings that literacy holds for groups of individuals (Zhang, Ollila, and Harvey, 1998, p. 182). As people mature and begin to associate themselves with some cultural or ethnic group, the ways they interpret and encode information about the world and their experience are 

determined by their cultural identity (Ferdman, 1991; Purcell-Gates, 1995 as quoted in Perez, 2004b, p. 4). Therefore, being literate is defined as not only being able to read and 

write the symbols, but also the ability to do so in a culturally appropriate manner (Perez, 

2004b, p. 5). Gee also argues that “the focus of literacy studies cannot be, and ought not to be, on language, or even literacy itself as traditionally construed. Rather the focus must be on social practices” (1990, p. 137). For him, understanding grammar and 

meaning requires knowing how to find the meanings “within specific Discourse models 

connected to the values and interests of specific Discourses.” He explains that 

understanding the values and interests of various “Discourses” is necessary for 

participation in them (Colombi & Schleppegrell, 2002, p. 7). As literacy is often explored in terms of how people interact with and use reading and writing, it is important to explore research within this context. Reder (1994) points to the fact that it is vital to consider how individuals use written materials in different            

> cultural contexts, how their interactions influence and are influenced by written materials,

and how participants interpret and give meaning to the texts and actions involved (p. 36)’.            

> Cross-cultural studies of literacy in different societies (e.g., Baker 1998; Hardman 1998;

Martin-Jones & Bhatt 1998) as well as in North American society (e.g., Farr & Guerra, 1995; Heath, 1983; Reder, 1987; Weinstein-Shr, 1993), illustrate very different ways in                      

> “For more information on Reder’s (1994) Practice Engagement Theory, please refer to the Theoretical Framework section in Chapter 1of this thesis.

29 

which literacy is used in everyday life. These culturally different ways of using literacy are what Scribner and Cole (1981) call /iteracy practices. For instance, reading in aheritage language class, the Qur’an at mosque, or a newspaper on the bus are examples of 

literacy practices. However, to be able to truly improve abilities within literacy, scholars 

such as Lave and Wenger (1991) and Reder (1994) argues that one must be an actively take part in the literacy practice at hand. The previous section discussed different ideas of literacy, from a cognitive ability 

to read and write, to a social function that is critical for participation in a variety of 

cultural contexts. Due to its focus on literacy as a concept that integrates social meaning and participation, the sociocultural approach allows for a well defined framework in terms of second generation immigrants struggling with their community language literacy abilities. The next sections will focus on research related to the challenges involved in becoming biliterate and maintaining a high level of biliteracy. 

> Biliteracy

Interestingly, even though there has been a plethora of research done in terms of literacy, the concept of biliteracy has been explored by only a few scholars (Hormberger,             

> 1989, 1990; McQuillan, 1996; 1998; Reyes, 2001; Tse, 2000). Reyes (2001) refers to

biliteracy as a concept that includes “mastery of the fundamentals of speaking, reading and writing in two linguistic symbols” as well as being able to construct meaning by “making relevant cultural and linguistic connections with print” (p. 98). Hornberger (1994) sees biliteracy as based on nine continua characterizing contexts for biliteracy, individual biliteracy, and the media of biliteracy with interrelationships extending throughout (p. 105-106). Chevalier (2004) also examines biliteracy as positioned on a              

> continuum -at one end of the continuum is the ‘ideal’ bilingual: educated, fluent and

fully literate in both languages. At the other end are bilinguals who use the spoken language mainly at home and who have no knowledge of the written language (Chevalier, 2004, section VI, para. 1). Thus, the question arises, if speaking and reading fluently is considered the “ideal” bilingual, then what does this mean for people who are stronger in one language than another? Would they still consider themselves bilingual? According 

to Lotherington (2003), “bilingualism is a vague descriptor. A fluent and capable 30 

bilingual is not necessarily biliterate, although in our highly literate world, concomitant 

literacy proficiencies are implicit in notions of language proficiency. Moreover, varied levels of language proficiencies in a person’s linguistic repertoire may or may not earn 

him or her the designation of bilingual, depending on social, educational, and political 

norms” (Lotherington, 2003, p. 202). In Ontario, the great majority of schools (except those offering French Immersion programs and those intended for French-speaking children) have English as the medium of instruction. Consequently, students, as a result of elementary, secondary and post-secondary education, will most likely have stronger literacy abilities in English than their community language. Despite the fact that community language speakers have a variety of skill levels, Chevalier argues that these 

speakers all share certain attributes. First, they are bilingual, and few, if any, bilinguals are equally proficient in two languages in all areas (Chevalier, 2004). However, even though they may not be equally fluent in both linguistic areas, they do use at least parts of their two languages. Second, community language learning reflects an on-going process of intergenerational language shift from the community language to the language of the host country. Although skill levels may vary, community language learners “share a lack of familiarity with the full range of stylistic registers available to the educated native speaker” (2004, section II, para. 2). In other words then, although languages and skills may vary across community language speakers, most children of immigrants find 

themselves limited in specific contexts of language use. 

Biliteracy — A Rare Occurrence Maintaining a high fluency in the minority language can be difficult in amultilingual country such as Canada. Indeed, “literacy seems to be one of the principle casualties in language shift” (McQuillan, 1996, p. 34). Unfortunately, having stronger oral rather than written communication skills in a community language seems to be the norm rather than an exception. In fact, cases of individuals who have become orally fluent and developed high levels of heritage language literacy are labeled “extreme” or “deviant” according to Patton (1987 as quoted from, Tse, 2001, p. 677). As a result, most studies have focused on the low levels of community language literacy abilities in 

> individuals.

31 Isajiw (1990) did a study on ethnic identity retention in regards to four ethnic groups - German, Jewish, Italian and Ukrainian. In all four groups, he found that a larger number of respondents could read their ethnic language than could write it. As well, the 

reading and writing abilities themselves decreased sharply from generation to generation. For Italians, for example, the decline from first to second generation was the sharpest, falling sixty percentage points for reading and sixty-two percent for writing (Isajiw, 1990, p. 52). Another study, which focused on Latino high school students found similar results. Garcia and Diaz (1992) found that over seventy-five percent of the participants understood Spanish and English equally well, but fewer than half could write the two languages with equal proficiency (as quoted from Tse, 2001, p. 679). It seems that even when literacy abilities are developed, bilinguals rarely develop 

a high level of literacy in the community language. Garcia (2002) specifically explored high levels of academic biliteracy concerning bilingual teachers in New York State. As teaching standards have increased, bilingual teachers now have to pass an exam which tests their bilingual abilities, and for the first time, advanced biliteracy is required of them. Sadly, in an area where fifty percent of people speak languages other than English at home (Garcia & Fishman, 1996), there is a shortage of qualified bilingual teachers (Garcia, 2002, p. 245). Similarly in Canada, there seems to also be a lack of qualified bilingual and biliterate teachers in regards to Indigenous language programs in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. Although there have been Indigenous Teacher Education programs at several of the universities, as well as community based programs in these provinces since the 1970’s, limited attention has been paid to the preparation of bilingual and biliterate teachers (Ahenakew, Blair, & Fredeen, 1994). In fact, many teachers working in First Nations schools have stopped using Indigenous languages for classroom instruction all together (Blair, 1997 as cited in Canadian Indigenous Languages and Literacy Development Institute, 2001, para. 6). In addition, there is also achronic shortage of bilingual (French/English teachers) in teacher preparation programs in Canada (Ontario College of Teachers, 1998, para. 1). Consequently, French 

Immersion and Extended French programs across the country suffer because of a lack of 

qualified teachers. Therefore, the lack of biliteracy will continue not only among future 32 indigenous students, but also those belonging to other minority languages, resulting in not 

only a language shift, but in some cases a disappearance of the language all together. Why is it so Difficult to Become Biliterate? As research shows, maintaining and/or developing community language literacy 

is far from the norm among youth and adults alike. Attaining biliteracy could thus be 

seen as a difficult task for people to achieve. Street (1984) shows how literacy is often constitutive of a society’s power structure. When literacy practices require taking part in that power structure, literacy and non-literacy tend to carry the strong social meanings associated with access and lack of access to that power structure and thereby impact the             

> social distribution of literacy in the society (Edelsky, 1991; Gee, 1990; Lemke, 1989;

Ogbu, 1990 as cited in Reder, 1994, p. 46). Therefore, Bourdieu’s (1991) concept of cultural capital plays a significant role in regards to the importance placed on literacy in general and literacy in English in particular. Lotherington (2003) argues that because society demands that the term literacy be narrowly constructed and expressed in terms of language proficiencies in specific and powerful languages (p. 202), other literacies, such as those that belong to a minority language, lose importance in multilingual countries 

such as Canada and the United States. As bilingualism is a topic of contention? in the 

United States, Reyes (2000) finds that although “many Latinos come to school with the natural potential to become biliterate, that potential frequently is undermined, dismissed, and ignored” (p. 119). Literacy in the context of Ontario is primarily focused on one of the two official languages - English and French. However, immigrants represent approximately twenty-

five percent of Ontario’s population, whereas about eighteen per cent of Ontarians have a

first language other than English or French (Ontario Ministry of Education, 2003, para. 4). According to The Report of the Expert Panel on Early Reading in Ontario, 2003: “this diversity in student backgrounds has many implications for early reading instruction. It is not, in itself, an obstacle to reading achievement, provided that the students have a solid foundation in their first language and support for attaining fluency 33 

in the language of instruction” (2003, para. 4). However, throughout my research, except for the heritage/international language classes, I have encountered very few Ministry initiatives that aid parents in creating this “solid foundation”. In fact, on December 6, 

2005 the Auditor General of Ontario discussed his concerns about the state of ESL support as well as how school boards actually spend much of their ESL funding on other 

academic and non-academic areas of the school. In addition, it was argued that the Ministry of Education should guarantee that every ESL student will continue to receive 

support until he or she has achieved a standard level of English proficiency rather than ending support when funding runs out (as is presently the case) (People for Education, 

2005, para. 2). Many researchers have shown that within the first few years of entering school, most bilingual students experience a rapid loss of their community language (Cummins, 1991; 2001; Wong Fillmore, 1991). This finding makes sense as schools provide little exposure to reading materials in minority languages (Jones, 2004; McQuillan, 1998; McQuillan & Au, 2002; Pucci, 1994). Thus, if we follow the notion that children need sustained contact with a language in order to acquire it (Gass & Selinker, 1994; Krashen, 1985), community language literacy would be very difficult to attain (Tse, 2001, p. 682). 

An area where minority language literacy can be acquired is within a heritage 

language (also known in Ontario as “International Language”) class. It would make sense that the more exposure students received in terms of literacy, the more apt they 

would be to retain it. However, many scholars have also found that the classes are 

plagued with unqualified teachers and poor pedagogy (Peng, 1996; Wang, 1996). Li (2005) and Shin (2005) both urge that teachers in Korean and Chinese heritage language schools respectively, should attempt to provide more interesting and creative classes instead of rote learning that is so often used. Unfortunately, many of these classes, especially within the context of Ontario, are what Feuerverger (1989) terms, “non-integrated”: only held after school hours, either in the late afternoon or on Saturday morning. In her research comparing non-integrated and integrated (incorporated into the

Thus, with most students in non-integrated programs feeling de-legitimized in terms of language and culture, it may be very difficult to attain a high level of literacy in such programs. According to Colombi and Schleppegrell (2002), “when literacy skills are 

taught in a language other than English, development frequently ends with initial literacy” (p. 4). As well, Cummins argues that in the case of subordinated groups, 

literacy programs that fail to focus on cultural and critical aspects of literacy and only stay within a functional literacy concentration are unlikely to succeed in building a high level of literacy (1994, p. 307). As a result, many of these students may build some initial literacy, but an academic level is impossible to reach. Academic language proficiency is one of three types of language proficiency described by Cummins (2001). This type of proficiency is the understanding of the less frequent vocabulary and the ability to infer and produce increasingly complex written and oral language. The second 

involves the mastery of discrete language skills which reflect specific phonological literacy and grammatical knowledge that students gain because of direct instruction and 

both formal and informal practice. Lastly, conversational fluency is the type of proficiency that the vast majority of native speakers of English have developed when they enter school at age five (2001, p. 65-66). Therefore, by speaking the community 

language at home and taking community language classes, students will be able to maintain a high level of conversational fluency within the register of the home. On the other hand, because speakers rarely get to use their community language in high level 

academic settings, this will result in them having limited academic vocabulary and literacy. Strong literacy skills also come from being exposed to and reading different types of print resources, such as books, magazines, comic books etc. Unfortunately, studies from the United States have shown that heritage language speakers often have extremely limited access to minority language reading materials at home, in school, and in the community (McQuillan, 1998). Research has shown that more access to books leads to more reading, and more reading results in higher levels of grammatical accuracy, a larger vocabulary, greater reading comprehension (Krashen, 1993). Therefore, McQuillan 35 

argues that one of the main challenges in preserving and developing heritage language 

literacy is increasing access to interesting, comprehensible community language texts in a

low risk environment (1998, p. 73). Ways to Achieve Biliteracy 

After exploring reasons why people find it difficult to achieve community language literacy, it is appropriate to examine the research that explains how people can 

maintain these skills. Williams and Capizzi Snipper state that in order to become a

balanced bilingual, four factors apply: 1) whether the children receive equal experiences in both languages; 2) whether children choose to use one language to the exclusion of the other; 3) outside influences, such as the value attached by mainstream society to the 

heritage language; 4) whether or not the native language is allowed or acceptable within the school system (1990, p. 40). Lucy Tse (2001) also found that a number of variables were related to becoming biliterate. The researcher examined specifically the reasons why a group of bilinguals born or raised in the United States were able to develop a high level of biliteracy. She found that a) the vitality of the heritage language and b) the literacy environment and 

experiences were what allowed for heritage language literacy to develop in these 

participants. For example, in order to build a positive attitude (i.e., vitality) towards their heritage language each participant had 1) a peer group that used the heritage language and introduced literacy related activities, thus helping them to form positive opinions about becoming literate; 2) contact with institutions that valued the language; and 3) parents who spoke the heritage language and encouraged its development (2001, p. 686). Tse also mentions how a literate environment plays an important role in building a foundation for biliteracy. All of the participants began to have literacy experiences at an early age and had access to heritage language literacy from many sources in different               

> contexts (i.e., store signs, religious texts, etc.) (2001, p. 691). As well, all of the

participants in her study had some sort of formal instruction in the heritage language, usually in an after school or Saturday program for three to five hours a week. Interestingly, the participants did not see the prestige in these classes until they noticed 36 them being offered either as an in-school course, or taken at the college level. This supports Feurverger’s (1989) finding that heritage language classes offered outside of school time produced a lowered perception of the language in the eyes of the enrolled students. In addition, many students took an active interest in improving their heritage language literacy because of ethnic identity issues. For instance, one participant, Ernesto, developed a desire to improve his Spanish because he saw it as an integral part of his emerging identity as a Chicano. Lastly, all of her participants had access to reading 

materials in the heritage language, and nearly all developed an interest in reading in the 

heritage language for pleasure (Tse, 2001, p. 695). 

McQuillan (1998) also found that heritage language classes which emphasize pleasure reading and other forms of comprehensible input worked well in improving literacy abilities in college students enrolled in Spanish for Native Speakers classes. In 

addition, Cho and Krashen (2000) also argued that one of the independent predictors of heritage language competence is reading. Finally, Cummins findings match those of Tse 

for he argues that extensive reading and immersion in a literate environment are strongly related to the development of reading comprehension (2001, p. 91). However, Cummins also brings up the point that some explicit instruction in terms of phonemic awareness is 

also important in developing decoding skills (2001, p. 92). Therefore reading comprehension is “best promoted by a broadly based program that combines extensive exposure to meaningful and varied texts with (a) some explicit phonemic awareness and phonics instruction, (b) instruction that encourages students to develop effective learning 

strategies for both decoding and comprehending text (meta-cognitive and meta-linguistic awareness)” (Cunningham, 1990; Iverson & Tunmer, 1993; Muniz-Swicegood, 1994; Tunmer & Chapman, 1990 as cited in Cummins, 2001, p. 94). The preceding sections have discussed biliteracy specifically in terms of 

community language literacy learning. There is consensus among researchers that 

achieving this literacy is very difficult because of lack of community language resources and time spent in community language classrooms. However, in the research that has explored successful biliterates, it remains clear that a high ethnolinguistic vitality, in addition to extensive reading, are key in community language maintenance. The next 37 section examines research that points out how important literacy or a lack there of, is in terms of bilingual identity. 

Literacy and Identity “Literacy touches us at our core in that part of ourselves that connects with the 

social world around us. It provides an important medium through which we interact with 

the human environment” (Ferdman, 1990, p. 181). In other words, being able to read and 

write is one the ways in which we identify with the world and ourselves. Gee (1996) 

clearly states that an individual’s identity is affected by both the ability and the inability to write. As a result, investigating just how people are caught in a dichotomous 

relationship with literacy — being fully literate in one of their languages and not literate in 

another — is significant in the area of language and identity. Other researchers examine literacy and identity less in terms of the individual, but more in regards to larger social and political contexts. Norton argues that how people understand their social relationships to each other and to the world is embedded in a

variety of social sites. Therefore, literacy and identity are “mutually constitutive” (1997, p. 411). Tse broadens this example by stating that social identity “is inextricable from broader political and social forces, although it is ultimately one’s perception and reaction 

to these influences that determines the degree of language and literacy development (Tse, 

2001, p. 681). Examples of such social and political forces may be the country’s political 

stance or a school’s stance on minority language use. As well, whether or not alanguage/cultural group has strong institutions, such as community centers, heritage language schools, media outlets (etc.) can all make a difference in terms of how a cultural group is perceived in the eyes of its members, affecting its vitality (Giles & Johnson, 1987) and consequently, creating environments in which minority languages and      

> literacies can either thrive or deteriorate.

As noted, there is a plethora of research regarding identity and literacy in terms of the individual and society as a whole; however, there exists much less in regards to cultural or ethnic identity and literacy, especially in a community language context. Much of the current research that does exist seems to focus more on identity in terms of reading and writing in an immigrant context, namely, English as a second language 38           

> (Hoffman, 1991; Kanno, 2003; Norton, 2000; Pavienko, 2000). Throughout my readings,

I encountered very little in terms of community language literacy and identity specifically. Generally, however, Bernardo Ferdman was one of the first people to relate cultural identity to literacy. He defines cultural identity as “the behaviors, beliefs, values, 

and norms” that a person uses to define himself or herself as a member of a particular 

cultural group (Ferdman, 1990, p. 182). Literacy, on the other hand, is regarded “as an 

essential part of a person’s conception of his/her culture and personhood - appropriate to the members of the ethnic group to which he or she belongs (Ferdman, 1991; Street, 1995 

from Li, 2000, p. 10). Therefore, when thinking of reading and writing in a multicultural 

context, we must be aware that what is termed ‘literacy’ in one group may be very different than what it is in another. Castell and Luke (1983) argue that “being ‘literate’ 

has always referred to having mastery over the processes by means of which culturally significant information is coded” (as cited in Ferdman, 1991, p. 186). Therefore, what one considers “texts” are different from culture to culture, resulting in different values 

and different ideas of what they view as literate behaviour. “An illiterate person is someone who cannot access (or produce) texts that are seen as significant within a given culture. That same person, in another cultural context, may be classified as being quite literate. When a number of cultures co-exist within the same society, it is more likely 

that we will encounter variant conceptions of what constitutes being literate” (Ferdman, 

# 1990, p. 186). 

Scholars such as Kenner (2004) and Saxena (1991) have carried out empirical studies examining students who are biliterate and how this impacts their identity. Saxena (1991) found that Punjabis in Southall, England were motivated by religious or nationalistic ideology in having their children learn the literacies of their home country. 

For example, learning to read Gurmukhi script was symbolic of the Sikh nation or the 

Punjabi cultural identity, while learning to read Davanagari script represented acommitment to Hindu cultural identity or pan-Indian identity (as cited in Blackledge, 

1999, p. 183). 

Other researchers have also explored the connection between literacy and cultural identity. Li (2000) investigated the relationship between literacy and cultural identity in aFilipino immigrant family in Canada. Through her ethnographic process, she found that 39 

literacy is not just an individual construct, but also one that involves family relationships that are embedded in cultural identity. Baynham (1995) pointed out that when people 

discuss their own writing everything they say is influenced by societal values and, all writing reflects identity and group affiliations. For instance, Camitta (1993) found that the writing produced by high school students reflected cultural values as well as the writer’s identity as defined by the culture. Bankston and Zhou (1995) researched the related topic ethnic identity and literacy. Vietnamese heritage language students who rated themselves as being able read and write very well in Vietnamese had higher 

academic achievement, more positive attitudes to school, and were more likely to identify          

> as Vietnamese than students who could not read in Vietnamese.

In all of the above research, students had a choice of literacies to use — their home 

language and English. Choosing to use different literacies at different times has been 

found to influence identity. Fishman’s theory of social meaning (1972) is used to describe social motivations underlying individuals’ preferences for using particular languages in multilingual contexts. For bilinguals, alternating and using their languages 

is seen in terms of social motivation to display greater or lesser attachments to social groups in which use of one language over the other is preferred (as cited in Reder, 1994, p. 45). This act of identity can also be seen in terms of literacy (Fishman, 1972; Reder 

and Green, 1983). These researchers have found that by investigating contexts in which multiple writing systems are in use, the social meanings associated with literacy choices may be understood in the same way as those associated with language choices. In fact, Ferdman (1990) argues that the acquisition of certain forms of literacy may eventually require the individual to redefine his or her cultural identity. Thus the question needs to be asked again, if literacy is missing in the community language, does this mean individuals have a more difficult time identifying with that culture? The previous sections included a discussion of research done in the area of literacy and identity. Studies have examined the two concepts in a monolingual setting, 

as well as in a multicultural context. Within a culturally diverse society, the definition of literacy becomes very different in each situational context, and thus, plays a pivotal role in the construction of identity. The research explored in this literature review shows that 

the topics of literacy and identity are extensive; however, there is a gap in terms of those 40 

who find themselves struggling with minority language literacy and how they identify themselves in the process. The next chapter will discuss which methodological approach I adopted to collect and analyze the data. Chapter 3Methodology and Design I believe that in order to understand the process of identity as a socially 

constructed and fluid concept that takes place and changes over time, I needed to adopt a

qualitative approach to data collection and analysis. As Denzin and Lincoln (2000) state, 

“qualitative researchers stress the socially constructed nature of reality, the intimate relationship between researcher and what is studied, and the situational constraints that 

shape inquiry...they seek answers to questions that stress how social experience is created and given meaning. In contrast, quantitative studies emphasize the measurement and analysis of causal relationships between variable, not processes” (2000, p. 8). Merriam (2002) also believes that within qualitative research there are “multiple constructions and interpretations of reality that are in flux and that change over time. Qualitative researchers are interested in understanding what those interpretations are at aparticular point in time and in a particular context” (2002, p. 4). As a result, a qualitative approach is an appropriate methodology to use in studying dynamic feelings and perceptions about language, literacy, and identity. Another factor in choosing a qualitative approach relates to my own involvement as aresearcher. This research area is very close to me because of my own experience as a ‘bilingual’ who is not biliterate. Thus in order to provide a fair representation of my participants’ opinions and experiences, I believe I have to be honest about my own. Esterberg (2002) states that qualitative researchers need to pay attention to the subjective nature of human life - not only the subjective experiences they are studying, but also the 

subjectivity of the researchers themselves (2002, p. 4). 

The qualitative paradigm allows for a range of data collection strategies. I believe that the technique of interviewing is the most effective in allowing me to gain insight into my participants’ perceptions and feelings on their language, literacy and identity. Often, identity is not only a personal quality, but it may also be imposed by others. Thus, 

simply observing a participant would have only given me a sense of their identity as seen through my eyes. By interviewing I have been able to have the opportunity to learn about 

41 42 

what I am unable to see as well as investigate alternative interpretations of what it is that 

I do see. This “is the special strength of interviewing in qualitative inquiry” (Glesne &

Peshkin, 1992, p. 65). Another reason interviewing is an appropriate technique to use is 

because it allows the researcher to get more than answers, participants can also offer 

explanations. By conversing with participants I have been able to get a better sense of 

their opinions and ideas, because as the researcher I can always ask, “why?”. Moreover, 

I have been able to find out more about the actual process of identity because participants 

have told me about not only their pasts, but also what they expect in their futures (ibid., p. 65). 

There are three different types of interviews including structured, semi-structured and unstructured interviews. In a structured interview, the questions and the order they |are presented in are set out ahead of time. In contrast, unstructured interviews simply follow a set of topics, but the questions and the order are not fixed (Merriam, 2002, p. 

13). I chose to do semi-structured interviews. This type of interview contains a list of 

guiding questions for the researcher; however, the order is not necessarily predetermined. As well, semi-structured interviews allow the researcher to respond to the participants’ answers, and ask follow-up questions that may not have been thought of previously. 

According to Merriam, semi-structured interviewing allows the emerging worldview of 

the respondent to shine through and gives the researcher new ideas on the topic (1988, p. 

74). 

Another method of interviewing that I used in my study is the focus group. Powell, Single and Lloyd (1996) define a focus group as “a group of individuals selected and assembled by researchers to discuss and comment on, from personal experience, the topic that is the subject of the research” (1996, p. 499). By gathering all of the participants together to discuss their perspectives about the same topic, I believe the study gained a greater richness than from only doing individual interviews. The individual interviews gave me a sense of an individual’s attitudes and experiences, but the focus group “elicit[ed] a multiplicity of views and emotional processes within a group context” (Gibbs, 1997, para. 7). By having interaction between all of the participants, they were able to not only discover how their experiences and ideas were similar or different, but also it gave them a chance to reexamine their own thoughts and feelings about the topic. 43 

Consequently, the focus group gave me, as the researcher, a better sense, of how 

language, literacy and identity affect these people’s lives as a whole. 

Research Design Objectives The main objective of my study is to discover how second generation Canadians, who are fluent in both English and their respective community languages, view their own identity. I examine specifically the role community language literacy, or lack there of, plays in the process of bilingual and ethnic identity construction. By exploring this topic a) I would like to contribute more to the connection between language and identity and b) ] hope to add to the understanding of the concept of bilingualism and whether the lack of biliteracy plays an integral role in judging if people feel they have the “right” to call themselves bilingual. In examining this topic, I decided to focus on identity as multi-faceted, multi-

dimensional, and socially constructed. Even though my main concern is how these 

people view themselves with regards to their community language and literacy, I am aware that language and ethnicity are not the only contributors to person’s identity. 

Family, friendships, education, and religion can all influence an identity. The fact that 

these participants were all born in Canada or arrived at a young age is an important factor 

in this study. Second generation Canadians, in regards to time, are more likely to be closer to their community language than third generation Canadians. Thus, the issues of 

language and identity may be more salient to this group of individuals because they were schooled in English, but grew up in a household where a minority language was spoken. 

As the study focuses on bilingual identity, not multilingual identity, it is vital to have 

participants who have parents that come from the same ethnic and language background. 

Lastly, all of my participants are between the ages of 18 and 35 and are either in college 

or university or have completed a degree already. Many researchers (Baker, 1995; Kondo-Brown, 2000; Tse, 1998) have found college to be a place and time in which many minority students undergo a major shift in their ethnic identity — from a strong identification with the majority culture to an interest in their own ethnic language 44 

(Kanno, 2003, p. 123). In addition, because the participants are either attending or finished university, they have a high level of English literacy. As a result, I can be certain that it is only the community language literacy that is limited for these participants. As a qualitative researcher, I am aware that my personal experiences and characteristics will influence the way I analyze and shape this study. As a second generation Polish-Canadian who cannot read and write my community language, I am in 

the same position as the participants. I believe to ignore this fact, and thus ignore my voice, would be detrimental to the integrity of this study. As a result, I write about my perceptions and lived experiences to situate myself throughout this study. 

Research Questions The following are the questions I address in my research: 1) How do the participants perceive and define themselves in terms of belonging to an ethnic minority in Toronto, Canada? e Do the participants identify with one culture more than the other? (For example, do they identify more with being Chinese than Canadian?) 

2) Does a lack of community language literacy impact the participants’ sense of “being 

bilingual” and thus, in turn, their identity? e How do the participants define the term ‘bilingual’? e Do the participants define themselves in terms of a bilingual identity? e Does having few or no community language literacy abilities affect my participants’      

> lives? If so, in what contexts?

3) What factors help to explain why the participants have developed a high level of oral proficiency in their community language, but not a high level of literacy? e In what contexts might the participants have had the opportunity to speak, read and write in their community language? e Did the participants receive any instruction in reading and writing their community language? 4) What advice would participants give to improve community language literacy in regards to educational and policy changes? 45 

e How could parents encourage their children to read and write in their community languages? e How could community language classes be more effective in terms of developing literacy? Methods of Data Collection
